summary:
Región de Los Lagos stands under Chile's national framework. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis, with no medical or surgical conditions attached. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations, and rules on access for trans visitors; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitors implementation.

The policy record has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers. In the 2025-26 rollback, the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombudsman for children.

Documented violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim. Institutional hostility is also visible inside state employment: Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.

There is no Los Lagos-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding. Outright International's Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, carries no division-specific information, so the national score is the basis for this division.

The division's recorded profile comes from Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026). Los Lagos accounts for 3.14% of nationally documented abuse cases, the fourth-largest regional share, with a +9.09% year-on-year rise in 2025. Nationally the report records a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest in 24 years; only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) fell, while the other 14 regions rose. The report reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate, which underpins the mid-range reading of the Los Lagos share. A low share is not evidence of safety.

The 2025 edition does not reproduce the 2024 share for this division.
tangentialFactors:
The regional figures are a ranking within a national surge, not a standalone measure. Los Lagos sits fourth of 16 regions by share of documented abuse cases, behind the two largest metropolitan regions, and its 2025 rise of 9.09% is smaller than the national increase of 27.1% because the two biggest regions declined while 14 regions grew. Movilh's own reading is that hatred is moving into areas with less public debate about LGBTIQ+ rights, so a comparatively modest share can coexist with worsening conditions on the ground.

The national backdrop against which a visitor to Los Lagos arrives is one of institutional retreat: equality and trans-rights bills stalled, non-discrimination reform rejected in parliament, and the Gender Identity Support Program stripped from the 2026 budget. The protective statutes remain in force, but the machinery that funded and defended them is thinner than the legal text suggests.

Violence risk documented nationally has included a fatal anti-trans killing in 2023 and a near-fatal group assault in the capital in September 2021; neither incident is located in Los Lagos, and no trans-specific killing in this division appears in the inventory.
localsOnly:
Residents of Región de Los Lagos access legal gender recognition through the national process under Gender Identity Law 21.120, available on self-determination since 2019 without medical or surgical requirements, and can obtain a third sex marker on birth certificates. Marriage and joint adoption rights, civil unions, and hate-crime aggravation for offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity all apply here as national law.

Residents deprived of liberty are covered by the Gendarmería de Chile protocol on recognition of assumed gender, segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations and trans visitor access, with a standing committee monitoring compliance. The protocol is a national instrument and applies in the region's detention facilities.

Reporting channels are those used to compile the Movilh figures: documented abuse cases are logged by the national diversity-rights organisation, which recorded 3,620 nationally in 2025. Residents also face a period in which the Gender Identity Support Program is unfunded for 2026 and non-discrimination law reform has been rejected by lawmakers.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Los Lagos-specific legal provision, incident, arrest, prosecution or enforcement action is sourced. The division's profile rests entirely on a national case table and on national statutes; whether the Gendarmería protocol is implemented in this region's facilities is not sourced here.

The 2024 share of national cases for this division is unresolved: the 2025 Movilh edition does not reproduce it, and no other source in the inventory supplies it. The 2026 Outright International dossier likewise carries no division-level data.

Not sourced for this division: regional access to gender-affirming healthcare, the presence or rules of gendered facilities, police practice toward trans people in Los Lagos, and any local hate-crime prosecution. The 2025 case figures are counts of documented complaints, not convictions.
